-- * For plain literal replacement of all occurrences, replace(src, from, to)
--   is simpler and does not use regex.
-- * Invalid regex or unknown flag raises an error.
query.explanation: `regexp_replace` substitutes text matching a POSIX regular expression, and by default only replaces the first match; the `'g'` flag makes it replace every match instead, which is why all the dashes turn into slashes here. Postgres’s regex support is built on POSIX syntax with its own extensions, not PCRE, so some patterns from other languages need adjusting.

questions.prompt: What does `name ~* '^jan'` test?

choices.text: Whether name starts with "jan", case-sensitively
Whether name starts with "jan", case-insensitively
Whether name contains "jan" anywhere, case-insensitively
Whether name does not start with "jan", case-insensitively

query.title: Pattern matching
query.syntax:
-- General form: POSIX regular expression match operators
-- string ~   pattern   -- matches, case-sensitive
-- string ~*  pattern   -- matches, case-insensitive
-- string !~  pattern   -- does NOT match, case-sensitive
-- string !~* pattern   -- does NOT match, case-insensitive

SELECT 'Postgres' ~  '^post';    -- false (case differs)
SELECT 'Postgres' ~* '^post';    -- true  (case ignored, anchored at start)
SELECT 'Postgres' ~* 'GRE';      -- true  (unanchored: matches anywhere)
SELECT 'Postgres' !~* '^sql';    -- true  (does not start with sql)

SELECT city FROM offices WHERE city ~* '^san ';

-- Gotchas:
-- Regex is unanchored by default; use ^ for start, $ for end.
-- LIKE/ILIKE must match the WHOLE string; ~ / ~* match any substring.
-- ILIKE 'abc%' is the LIKE equivalent of ~* '^abc'.
-- Escape metacharacters (. * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \) to match literally.
-- NULL ~ 'x' yields NULL, not false.
query.explanation: `~` and `~*` are Postgres operator syntax for POSIX regular expression matching, with the star variant folding case before comparing. This gives you full regex power (anchors, character classes, quantifiers) in a `WHERE` clause, well beyond what `LIKE`/`ILIKE`’s wildcard-only patterns can express.

questions.prompt: Postgres supports both `LIMIT 10` and the SQL-standard `FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY` to cap a result set.

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;
SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
query.explanation:
LIMIT vs FETCH FIRST

`LIMIT`/`OFFSET` is the traditional Postgres (and MySQL) idiom, while `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` is the ANSI SQL:2008 standard phrasing; Postgres accepts both and they behave the same way. Reaching for the standard form can matter for portability if the same query needs to run unmodified against, say, Oracle or DB2.

questions.prompt: `a IS DISTINCT FROM b` is preferred over `a <> b` when either side might be `NULL`. Why?

choices.text: It treats NULL as an empty string, so NULL and '' are equal
It treats NULL as a comparable value, so it always returns true or false
It raises an error instead of returning NULL on NULL input
It can use an index on either column, while <> cannot

query.title: Comparison operators
query.syntax:
-- General form: NULL-safe comparison
-- expr IS DISTINCT FROM expr      -- like <>, but NULL-aware
-- expr IS NOT DISTINCT FROM expr  -- like =,  but NULL-aware

-- Ordinary comparison returns NULL if either side is NULL
SELECT 5 <> NULL;                          -- NULL (unknown)
SELECT NULL = NULL;                        -- NULL (unknown)

-- NULL-aware comparison always returns true or false
SELECT 5 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;            -- true
SELECT NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;         -- false
SELECT NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL;     -- true

-- Find rows whose value changed, including to or from NULL
SELECT id FROM orders o JOIN orders_audit h USING (id)
WHERE o.status IS DISTINCT FROM h.status;

-- Gotchas:
-- * WHERE x <> 'shipped' silently skips rows where x is NULL;
--   WHERE x IS DISTINCT FROM 'shipped' includes them.
-- * NULL is not treated as ''; '' IS DISTINCT FROM NULL is true.
-- * No error is raised on NULL input; the result is just never NULL.
-- * IS NOT DISTINCT FROM usually can't use a plain btree index the way
--   '=' can, so prefer '=' when columns are NOT NULL.
-- * For a single value use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead.
query.explanation: Ordinary `<>` follows three-valued logic: comparing anything against `NULL`, including another `NULL`, yields `NULL` rather than `true` or `false`, which silently drops rows from a `WHERE` clause. `IS DISTINCT FROM` treats `NULL` as a comparable value, so it always returns a definite `true`/`false`, making it the safe choice for change-detection logic.

questions.prompt: What does `CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad', 'ok', 'happy');` create?

choices.text: A CHECK constraint you attach to each column that needs it
A new type whose values are limited to the listed labels
A small lookup table holding those three labels as rows
A text domain that sorts its labels alphabetically

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('sad', 'ok', 'happy');
CREATE TABLE t (current_mood mood);
query.explanation: Postgres lets you define a genuine enumerated type once, with `CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM`, and then reuse it across any number of columns or tables, with values compared and sorted by their declared list order rather than alphabetically. This is a distinct feature from a `CHECK (col IN (...))` constraint, which only guards one column at a time and has no shared, sortable type identity.

questions.prompt: What does `CREATE TYPE point_2d AS (x int, y int);` define?

choices.text: An alias for the built-in geometric point type
A composite type with named, typed fields x and y
A table named point_2d with columns x and y
A two-element integer array type, int[2]

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
CREATE TYPE point_2d AS (x int, y int);
SELECT (1, 2)::point_2d;
query.explanation:
Composite types

A composite type groups several named fields into one reusable structured type, similar to a lightweight struct, that you can use as a column type, a function’s return type, or a cast target. Every table also implicitly has a composite type matching its own row shape, which is why row-level casts like `SELECT t.*::text` work.

questions.prompt: What does `CREATE DOMAIN positive_int AS integer CHECK (VALUE > 0);` let you do?

choices.text: An alias for integer; the CHECK is only documentation
A reusable integer type that enforces the CHECK wherever it is used
A new type that must be cast explicitly to mix with integer
A constraint added to every existing integer column

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
CREATE DOMAIN positive_int AS integer CHECK (VALUE > 0);
CREATE TABLE t (qty positive_int);
query.explanation:
CREATE DOMAIN

A domain wraps a base type with extra constraints (here, a `CHECK` referencing the special `VALUE` keyword) and packages that as one named type you can reuse across many tables. It centralizes the validation rule in one place instead of copy-pasting the same `CHECK (qty > 0)` onto every table that has a quantity column.

questions.prompt: `\copy` and `COPY` always run in exactly the same place: on the Postgres server.

query.title: Bulk data import and export in PostgreSQL
query.syntax:
-- Server-side form (SQL command):
COPY table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)];
COPY table_name | (query) TO 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)];

-- Client-side form (psql meta-command, one line, no trailing semicolon needed):
\copy table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)]
\copy (query) TO 'path' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)]

-- Examples:
COPY invoices TO '/var/lib/postgresql/out/invoices.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);
\copy invoices FROM 'invoices_in.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * COPY with a file name: the file is read/written by the server process,
--   path resolved on the server's filesystem, using the server OS account's permissions.
-- * COPY with a file needs superuser or membership in pg_read_server_files /
--   pg_write_server_files; PROGRAM needs pg_execute_server_program.
-- * \copy: psql opens the file itself as the client user, then streams the data
--   to the server via COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT. Path is relative to psql's
--   working directory.
-- * COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT transfers data over the connection (used by drivers).
-- * Options: FORMAT text|csv|binary, DELIMITER, NULL, HEADER, QUOTE, ESCAPE.
-- * COPY is not a normal INSERT: it is fast, and triggers fire but rules do not.
-- * Whole load fails if any row is bad (unless ON_ERROR is set in newer versions).
query.explanation: Plain SQL `COPY` reads or writes a file on the Postgres server’s own filesystem and requires server-level file permissions, which is a nonstarter for a managed/hosted database you cannot SSH into. `\copy` is a psql-only wrapper that streams the data through the client connection instead, letting you load a file that only exists on your local machine.

questions.prompt: Why is `COPY` typically much faster than issuing many individual `INSERT` statements for the same rows?

choices.text: It skips CHECK and foreign key constraints during the load
It loads rows in one bulk stream instead of one planned statement per row
It disables indexes and rebuilds them once at the end
It runs the inserts in parallel across several worker processes

query.title: Data loading
query.syntax:
-- General form
COPY table_name [(col1, col2, ...)]
  FROM { 'server_file' | STDIN | PROGRAM 'cmd' }
  [WITH (FORMAT csv|text|binary, HEADER, DELIMITER ',', NULL '')];
COPY { table_name | (SELECT ...) } TO { 'file' | STDOUT };

-- Load a CSV into a table (one command, rows streamed in)
COPY products (sku, name, price)
  FROM '/srv/import/products.csv'
  WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);

-- Export query results
COPY (SELECT sku, price FROM products WHERE price > 50)
  TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);

-- psql client-side variant: reads a file on YOUR machine
-- \copy products FROM 'products.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

-- Gotchas:
-- * Server-side files need superuser or pg_read_server_files /
--   pg_write_server_files; use \copy or STDIN otherwise.
-- * Parsed and planned once, not once per row.
-- * Constraints, triggers and index updates still happen per row.
-- * One bad row aborts the whole COPY by default
--   (PG 17+: ON_ERROR ignore for data type errors).
-- * For big loads: drop indexes/FKs first, recreate after;
--   raise maintenance_work_mem; run ANALYZE afterward.
-- * FREEZE option works only if the table was created or
--   truncated in the same transaction.
query.explanation: Each individual `INSERT` pays the cost of parsing, planning, and a network round trip. `COPY` instead streams many rows through a dedicated bulk-loading code path in one pass, still enforcing constraints and firing row-level triggers as it goes, which is why it is the standard tool for loading CSV exports rather than generating thousands of INSERT statements.

questions.prompt: What does `pg_typeof(3.14)` return?

choices.text: 'float4'
'numeric'
'double precision'
'int'

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
SELECT pg_typeof(3.14);   -- numeric
SELECT pg_typeof(3.14::real); -- real
query.explanation:
pg_typeof()

`pg_typeof` reports the actual resolved data type Postgres assigned to any expression, which is a quick way to confirm what type a literal, column, or function result really is without guessing. An unqualified decimal literal like `3.14` defaults to `numeric`, not a floating-point type, unless you explicitly cast it.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT nextval('my_seq');` do to the sequence `my_seq`?

choices.text: Only previews the next value without changing sequence state
Advances the sequence and returns the new current value
Returns the next value, advancing only if the transaction commits
Returns the last value this session got from the sequence

query.title: PostgreSQL sequences
query.syntax:
-- General forms
nextval(regclass)  -> bigint
currval(regclass)  -> bigint
lastval()          -> bigint
setval(regclass, bigint [, is_called boolean]) -> bigint

-- Example setup
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no START 100 INCREMENT 5;

SELECT currval('order_no');      -- error if nextval not yet called in this session
SELECT setval('order_no', 500);  -- next nextval returns 505
SELECT setval('order_no', 500, false); -- next nextval returns 500
SELECT lastval();                -- latest value returned by nextval in this session, any sequence

-- Typical use
INSERT INTO orders(id, item) VALUES (nextval('order_no'), 'pen');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence state is shared by all sessions; currval/lastval are session-local.
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are not rolled back
--   on ROLLBACK, so gaps in values are normal.
-- * Concurrent sessions each receive distinct values, never blocked by
--   other transactions' uncommitted calls.
-- * CACHE n makes a session preallocate values; other sessions may see
--   out-of-order values.
-- * Argument is regclass: a quoted name, resolved via search_path;
--   use 'schema.seq' to be explicit.
-- * serial / identity columns use a sequence behind the scenes.
query.explanation: Sequences are independent, transaction-spanning counter objects. `nextval()` has a side effect: it permanently advances the counter (even if the surrounding transaction later rolls back, which is intentional, so concurrent transactions never collide on the same value) and returns the new value. `currval()` just re-reads the value your own session last obtained, without advancing anything.

questions.prompt: A sequence value obtained with `nextval()` is given back to the sequence if the transaction that called it rolls back.

query.title: Database sequences and transactions
query.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_name [INCREMENT BY n] [START WITH n] [CACHE n] [CYCLE];
SELECT nextval('seq_name');   -- advance and return the new value
SELECT currval('seq_name');  -- last value nextval returned in THIS session
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100);         -- set current value explicitly
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100, false);  -- next nextval returns 100

-- Example
CREATE SEQUENCE invoice_no START 500;
CREATE TABLE invoice (id bigint DEFAULT nextval('invoice_no'), note text);
INSERT INTO invoice (note) VALUES ('first');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are designed so that
--   concurrent sessions never block each other on nextval.
-- * Consider how the effect of nextval interacts with transaction
--   commit/abort, and what that means for numbering continuity.
-- * Other causes of unused numbers: failed INSERTs, CACHE preallocation,
--   crash recovery.
-- * currval errors if nextval was not yet called in the session.
-- * serial / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY columns use sequences internally,
--   so they follow the same rules.
-- * Do not rely on sequences for gap-free numbering; use a separate
--   counter table with row locking if that is required.
query.explanation: Sequence advancement is deliberately exempt from transactional rollback: if it were not, two concurrent transactions could both be handed the same "next" value while waiting to see which one commits, defeating the entire purpose of a sequence. This is why gaps in a `SERIAL` primary key after aborted inserts are completely normal, not a bug.

questions.prompt: What does `CREATE TABLE managers () INHERITS (employees);` set up?

choices.text: A managers table whose rows reference employees by foreign key
A child table that gets employees' columns and shows up in its queries
A copy of employees' columns, with no link between the tables afterwards
A table sharing employees' storage, so rows appear in both

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.explanation: Postgres table inheritance is a genuine, native feature (distinct from foreign keys or views) that lets a child table automatically pick up its parent’s columns and be included in queries against the parent by default. It predates and partly overlaps with declarative partitioning, but inheritance is more general and does not require the child ranges to be non-overlapping.

questions.prompt: What does `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()` set up?

choices.text: A default fixed to the moment the table was created
A default that calls now() when an insert omits the column
A column refreshed with now() on every UPDATE
A NOT NULL column that always holds the insert time

query.title: Column defaults in table definitions
query.syntax:
-- General form
-- column_name data_type [ DEFAULT default_expr ] [ constraints ]
-- default_expr is a value expression evaluated per row at INSERT time
-- whenever the column is not supplied (omitted or DEFAULT keyword).

CREATE TABLE ticket (
  id        BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  status    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  priority  INT DEFAULT 3,
  opened_on DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- Default applies: column omitted, or DEFAULT keyword used
INSERT INTO ticket (priority) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO ticket (status, priority) VALUES (DEFAULT, 2);

-- Change or remove a default later (affects only future inserts)
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority SET DEFAULT 5;
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority DROP DEFAULT;

-- Gotchas
-- * An explicit NULL is stored as NULL; the default is NOT used.
-- * A default does not imply NOT NULL; add that constraint separately.
-- * A default is not applied by UPDATE (use a trigger for that).
-- * Volatile functions (random(), clock_timestamp()) run per row;
--   now() returns the current transaction's start time.
-- * Defaults cannot reference other columns or contain subqueries.
-- * Without DEFAULT, an omitted column becomes NULL.
query.explanation: A column `DEFAULT` is not limited to a constant, it can be any expression, including a function call, evaluated fresh for each row that omits an explicit value on insert. `DEFAULT now()` is the standard way to stamp a "created at" column without every application code path having to remember to set it.

questions.prompt: What does `gen_random_uuid()` return?

choices.text: A time-ordered UUID built from the current clock
A randomly generated UUID value
The UUID of the current session
A deterministic UUID based on the table name

query.title: UUID generation in PostgreSQL
query.syntax:
-- General form: a function call returning a value of type uuid
--   <function_name>()

-- Example: using a UUID generator as a column default
CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id    uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT <uuid_function>(),
    label text
);

INSERT INTO invoices (label) VALUES ('march') RETURNING id;

-- Call it directly in a query:
SELECT <uuid_function>();

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * The result has type uuid (128-bit), shown as 8-4-4-4-12 hex digits.
-- * Core Postgres (13+) provides gen_random_uuid() with no extension needed;
--   older versions needed the pgcrypto extension.
-- * Newer versions (18+) also add uuidv4() and uuidv7(); check the docs
--   for what each version-specific function guarantees.
-- * The uuid-ossp extension offers other generators, e.g. uuid_generate_v1(),
--   uuid_generate_v3()/v5() (namespace + name based).
-- * Each call is evaluated per row when used in DEFAULT or SELECT lists.
-- * The ordering of generated values affects index locality on a primary key.
query.explanation: `gen_random_uuid()` produces a random version-4 UUID and, as of Postgres 13, is built into core (`pgcrypto`’s older `gen_random_uuid()` and the `uuid-ossp` extension’s `uuid_generate_v4()` served the same purpose before that). UUID primary keys avoid the "guessable sequential id" and cross-database-merge problems a `SERIAL` key can have, at the cost of larger index entries.

questions.prompt: What does `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;` do?

choices.text: Turns on encryption at rest for this database's tables
Installs an optional package of functions and types into this database
Downloads pgcrypto from the network and compiles it
Loads pgcrypto server-wide, for every database at once

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
query.explanation: Postgres ships with a large catalog of optional extensions (cryptographic functions, trigram text search, UUID generators, and more) that are not enabled by default; `CREATE EXTENSION` registers one into the current database, exposing its functions/types/operators. This modular design keeps a fresh database’s catalog small until you explicitly opt into what you need.

questions.prompt: Which psql meta-command lists the extensions currently installed in the database?

choices.text: \dx
\df
\dn
\dt

query.title: psql meta-commands
query.syntax:
-- General form (run inside psql, not as SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S+] [pattern]
-- The letter after \d picks the kind of object to list.
-- Suffix + adds more detail (size, description, etc.).
-- Suffix S includes system objects.
-- pattern is an optional name filter; supports * and ?.

-- Examples:
--   \dv+ report_*     -- views whose names start with report_, with detail
--   \dT               -- user-defined data types

-- Common letters in the family:
--   \d name   describe one relation (columns, indexes)
--   \dt       tables
--   \dv       views
--   \di       indexes
--   \ds       sequences
--   \dn       schemas
--   \df       functions
--   \du       roles
--   \dT       data types
--   \dE       foreign tables
--   \l        databases (not a \d form)

-- Gotchas:
--   * Letters are case-sensitive: \dt and \dT differ.
--   * Meta-commands are psql features, not server SQL;
--     they work by querying the system catalogs.
--   * Use psql -E to echo the SQL a meta-command runs.
--   * Another letter in this family covers installed
--     extensions; check \? for the full list.
--   * Without a pattern, only objects visible on the
--     search_path are listed for many kinds.
query.explanation: `\dx` lists every extension registered in the current database along with its installed version, which is a quick sanity check before relying on an extension-provided function like `gen_random_uuid()` or `similarity()` in a query.

questions.prompt: What problem do dollar-quoted string literals like `$$...$$` solve?
questions.code: SELECT $$It's a string with an apostrophe$$;

choices.text: They interpolate $-prefixed variables into the string
They let a string contain single quotes without escaping them
They make the string case-insensitive in comparisons
They are the only way to write a multi-line string literal

query.title: String literals and quoting
query.syntax:
-- General form: $tag$ ... $tag$  (tag is optional, may be empty)
-- Text between the delimiters is taken literally: no escape processing,
-- single quotes and backslashes need no doubling.
SELECT $$O'Brien's book$$;          -- O'Brien's book
SELECT 'O''Brien''s book';          -- same value, standard quoting

-- Tagged form lets you nest dollar quotes (e.g. function bodies)
CREATE FUNCTION greet(name text) RETURNS text AS $fn$
  SELECT 'Hi, ' || name || $q$ -- it's $$ fine $$ here$q$;
$fn$ LANGUAGE sql;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Tags are case-sensitive: $Tag$ ... $tag$ do not match.
-- * Tag follows identifier rules, no $ inside it; $1 is a parameter, not a quote.
-- * No variable interpolation: $$x = $var$$ is just text.
-- * Backslashes are literal: $$a\nb$$ is 4 chars (a, \, n, b).
-- * Result type is unknown/text like any literal; no effect on collation
--   or case sensitivity of comparisons.
-- * Multi-line strings also work with ordinary '...' literals.
-- * A dollar-quote following an identifier char needs whitespace: x$$..$$ fails.
query.explanation: A single-quoted literal containing an apostrophe needs escaping (doubling it), which gets unreadable fast inside larger blocks like function bodies. Dollar-quoting, `$$...$$` or a tagged `$tag$...$tag$` to allow nested dollar-quoted blocks, treats everything between the markers as literal text with no escaping needed, which is why it is the standard way to write `plpgsql` function bodies.

questions.prompt: What does `INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6);` do?

choices.text: Inserts only the last row, (5, 6)
Inserts three separate rows in one statement
Raises a syntax error, VALUES only accepts one row
Inserts one row with six columns

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
INSERT INTO t (a, b)
VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6);
query.explanation:
Multi-row VALUES

The `VALUES` clause of an `INSERT` accepts any number of comma-separated row groups, each becoming its own inserted row, planned and executed as a single statement. This is both more concise and generally faster than issuing one `INSERT` per row, since it avoids the per-statement parse/plan overhead N times over.

questions.prompt: What does `TABLE orders;` do on its own, with no SELECT keyword?

choices.text: It is a syntax error, TABLE cannot start a statement
It is shorthand equivalent to SELECT * FROM orders
It lists the orders table's column definitions, like \d
It locks orders for the rest of the transaction

query.title: Query syntax
query.explanation: `TABLE name` is a small Postgres convenience: a standalone statement equivalent to `SELECT * FROM name` with no filtering or projection. It also composes inside a larger query, e.g. `TABLE orders UNION TABLE archived_orders`, which reads more tersely than spelling out `SELECT * FROM` twice.

questions.prompt: What does a standalone `VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b');` statement produce?

choices.text: An error, since VALUES is only valid inside an INSERT
An ad hoc result set of rows, with no backing table required
A temporary table named values holding those two rows
One row holding both tuples as a two-element array

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.explanation:
Standalone VALUES

`VALUES` is not limited to `INSERT`, it can stand on its own as a complete query producing literal rows on the fly, or be used as a subquery/CTE source. This is handy for constructing small lookup tables or test fixtures inline without a real `CREATE TABLE`.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1, 2, 3]);` produce?

choices.text: One row containing the array [1, 2, 3]
Three separate rows: 1, 2, and 3
The number 3 (the array length)
An error, unnest only works on jsonb

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1, 2, 3]);
SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY['a','b']) AS t(label);
query.explanation:
unnest()

`unnest` is a set-returning function that flips an array "sideways" into one row per element, the inverse operation of `array_agg`. It is the standard way to join an array column against another table, since you cannot directly `JOIN` on an array value without first expanding it into rows.

questions.prompt: `array_agg(product)` is used as an aggregate function in a GROUP BY. What does it do?
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, array_agg(product) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

choices.text: Collects the distinct values in the group into an array
Collects every value in the group into a single array
Concatenates the products into one comma-separated string
Wraps each product in its own one-element array

query.title: Aggregate functions
query.syntax:
-- General form: collect input values (including NULLs) into an array
array_agg(expression [ORDER BY sort_expr [ASC|DESC]])

-- One array per group
SELECT dept_id, array_agg(employee_name)
FROM staff
GROUP BY dept_id;
-- dept_id | array_agg
--       1 | {Ana,Ben,Ana}

-- Control element order inside the array
SELECT team, array_agg(score ORDER BY score DESC)
FROM results
GROUP BY team;

-- Variations & gotchas:
-- * Duplicates are kept; use array_agg(DISTINCT x) to drop them.
-- * NULL inputs become NULL elements; filter with
--   array_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL).
-- * Without ORDER BY, element order is unspecified.
-- * With no input rows, the result is NULL, not '{}';
--   use COALESCE(array_agg(x), '{}').
-- * Array inputs produce a multidimensional array (all must match size).
-- * For a delimited text string instead, use string_agg(x, ', ').
query.explanation: `array_agg` is the reverse of `unnest`: instead of collapsing rows into a single delimited string like `STRING_AGG`, it packs them into a genuine Postgres array value, preserving each element’s original type rather than converting everything to text. Like `STRING_AGG`, it accepts an `ORDER BY` inside the call to control element order.

questions.prompt: What does the psql meta-command `\!` do?

choices.text: Re-runs the previous query, like !! in a shell
Runs a shell command without leaving the psql session
Cancels the query that is currently running
Forces psql to quit, discarding unsaved input

query.title: psql meta-commands
query.syntax:
-- General form (psql client only, not SQL; no trailing semicolon)
\! [ command ]

-- Runs an OS shell command and returns to the psql prompt
\! ls -l /var/backups
\! date

-- With no argument: starts an interactive subshell;
-- type 'exit' to come back to psql
\!

-- Example: check a file before importing it
\! head -n 3 /data/orders.csv
\copy orders FROM '/data/orders.csv' CSV HEADER

-- Gotchas:
-- * Runs on the CLIENT machine, not the database server
-- * The rest of the line is passed to the shell unchanged
--   (psql does not expand :variables or handle quoting)
-- * The shell comes from $SHELL (default /bin/sh); Windows uses cmd.exe
-- * Cannot be used inside a single-line \\ separated list reliably;
--   put it on its own line
-- Related: \cd dir changes the client working directory,
--   \setenv NAME value sets an env var for child processes,
--   \g | cmd pipes a query's output to a shell command
query.explanation: `\!` hands its argument off to your operating system shell and prints the result inline, without disconnecting from Postgres, which is convenient for checking a local file or running a quick command mid-session. With no argument, it drops you into an interactive subshell you can exit to return to psql.

questions.prompt: What does `\i setup.sql` do inside psql?

choices.text: Imports setup.sql's rows into a table, like \copy
Runs the SQL commands in setup.sql as if you typed them
Shows the contents of setup.sql without running it
Runs setup.sql in a separate session in the background

query.title: PostgreSQL interactive terminal basics
query.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not sent to the server):
--   \meta-command [arguments]

-- Commands that take a file name:
\i  filename        -- \include
\ir filename        -- \include_relative (path relative to the current script)
\copy table FROM 'file' ...   -- client-side bulk data load/export
\o  filename        -- send query output to a file
\e  [filename]      -- open an editor

-- Examples with other names:
\i  /tmp/migrations/001_schema.sql
\ir ../seed/data.sql

-- Related, from the shell rather than inside psql:
--   psql -f file.sql dbname      (run a file, then exit)
--   psql -c 'SELECT 1' dbname    (run one command string)

-- Notes and gotchas:
-- * Backslash commands are handled by psql itself, not by the server.
-- * Relative paths in \i resolve against psql's current working directory;
--   use \ir inside nested scripts to resolve against the calling script.
-- * Errors in a file do not stop it by default; set ON_ERROR_STOP to on to abort.
-- * Files are read on the client machine, not the server.
-- * \copy moves data rows; it does not execute SQL statements found in a file.
-- * Use \? to list all meta-commands and \? variables for settings.
query.explanation: `\i` reads a file from the local filesystem (the client machine, same as `\copy`) and feeds its contents into psql line by line, exactly as though you had pasted the script in yourself. It is the standard way to replay a saved `.sql` file, including one containing other meta-commands.

questions.prompt: What does `pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('orders'))` return?

choices.text: The total size in bytes as a bigint, including indexes
The size formatted as a human-readable string like "24 MB"
A readable size such as "24 MB", excluding indexes and TOAST
The estimated row count, formatted like "24k rows"

query.title: System administration functions
query.syntax:
-- General form
pg_size_pretty(bigint | numeric) -> text   -- e.g. '8192 bytes', '24 MB'
pg_total_relation_size(regclass) -> bigint  -- table + indexes + TOAST
pg_relation_size(regclass [, fork text]) -> bigint  -- main fork only by default
pg_table_size(regclass) -> bigint           -- table + TOAST, no indexes
pg_indexes_size(regclass) -> bigint         -- all indexes on the table

-- Examples
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('invoices'));
-- e.g. '156 MB' (text)

SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size(oid))   AS data,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(oid)) AS idx
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- Gotchas
-- pg_size_pretty returns text: sort by the raw bigint, not the
--   pretty string ('9 MB' > '10 GB' as text).
-- Units are powers of 1024 (kB, MB, GB, TB, PB).
-- pg_size_bytes('1.5 GB') converts back to bigint.
-- pg_database_size('mydb') sizes a whole database.
-- Sizes are on-disk bytes, not row counts; use
--   pg_class.reltuples for an estimated row count.
query.explanation: `pg_total_relation_size` returns a raw byte count (table plus indexes plus TOAST), which is exact but unreadable at a glance. `pg_size_pretty` wraps any such byte count and formats it with the most sensible unit (kB, MB, GB), which is why the two are almost always used together in monitoring queries.

questions.prompt: What does `pg_database_size('mydb')` return?

choices.text: The size of mydb as readable text, such as "8 MB"
The total on-disk size of the mydb database, in bytes
The configured size limit for mydb, in bytes
The size of mydb's data, excluding its indexes, in bytes

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size('mydb'));
query.explanation:
pg_database_size()

`pg_database_size` sums the on-disk footprint of every table, index, and other object belonging to the named database, returned in bytes. It is commonly wrapped in `pg_size_pretty()` for a readable report, and is a cheap way to track database growth over time without walking every relation individually.

questions.prompt: What does `NULLIF(quantity, 0)` return when `quantity` is 0?

choices.text: NULL
An error

query.title: Conditional expressions
query.syntax:
-- General form
NULLIF(value1, value2)
-- Returns NULL if value1 = value2; otherwise returns value1.
-- Equivalent to: CASE WHEN value1 = value2 THEN NULL ELSE value1 END

-- Example: avoid division-by-zero errors
SELECT total_cost / NULLIF(units_sold, 0) AS unit_price
FROM sales;
-- units_sold = 0  -> divisor is NULL -> result is NULL (no error)

-- Example: treat empty strings as missing
SELECT NULLIF(trim(nickname), '') AS nickname FROM members;
-- '' -> NULL ; 'Sam' -> 'Sam'

-- Combine with COALESCE to supply a fallback
SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(region, 'n/a'), 'Unknown') FROM offices;

-- Gotchas:
-- * NULLIF(5, 7) returns 5 (first argument, unchanged).
-- * NULLIF(NULL, 3) returns NULL; NULLIF(4, NULL) returns 4
--   (comparison with NULL is never true).
-- * Arguments must be comparable types; result type is that of the first argument.
-- * Not the inverse of COALESCE: COALESCE replaces NULLs, NULLIF creates them.
query.explanation: `NULLIF(a, b)` returns `NULL` when the two arguments are equal, and otherwise returns `a` unchanged. It is most often reached for to avoid a division-by-zero error: `total / NULLIF(quantity, 0)` turns a would-be error into a clean `NULL` result whenever `quantity` is zero.

questions.prompt: What does `GREATEST(3, 7, 2)` return?

choices.text: An array of all three

query.title: SQL conditional expressions
query.syntax:
-- General form
GREATEST(value [, ...])
LEAST(value [, ...])

-- Examples
SELECT LEAST(10, 4, 8);            -- picks from the list of arguments
SELECT GREATEST('apple', 'pear');  -- works on text using collation ordering
SELECT GREATEST(price, 0) FROM items;  -- per-row clamp to a floor

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Takes one or more expressions; returns a single scalar value, not an array.
-- * All arguments must resolve to a common data type (same rules as UNION/CASE);
--   mixing int and numeric promotes to numeric.
-- * NULL arguments are ignored; the result is NULL only if ALL arguments are NULL.
--   (This differs from the MAX()/MIN() aggregates' behavior across rows? No: those
--   also skip NULLs, but they work over rows, not over an argument list.)
-- * GREATEST/LEAST compare values within one row; MAX/MIN aggregate across rows.
-- * To compare values from an array, use an aggregate or unnest:
--     SELECT max(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[5,9,1]) AS x;
query.explanation: `GREATEST` and `LEAST` take any number of comparable arguments and return the largest or smallest, skipping `NULL` values unless every argument is `NULL` (in which case the result is `NULL`). They are handy for clamping a value, e.g. `GREATEST(price, 0)` to prevent a negative price, without a `CASE` expression.

questions.prompt: What does `to_char(NOW(), 'YYYY-MM-DD')` produce?

choices.text: A date value with the time of day stripped off
The date formatted as a string using the given pattern
An error, because to_char only formats numbers
A string in the session's DateStyle, ignoring the pattern

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
to_char(timestamp, 'YYYY-MM-DD')
to_char(1234.5, 'FM9999.00')
query.explanation:
to_char() formatting

`to_char` converts a date/time or numeric value into a formatted `text` string using a template mini-language (`YYYY`, `MM`, `DD`, `HH24`, and dozens more tokens), which is far more flexible than relying on a client library or the default output format. It has a numeric counterpart pattern language too, for formatting currency-style output.

questions.prompt: What is `to_date('2024-05-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD')` used for?

choices.text: Formatting a date as text using the given pattern
Parsing text into a date using the given format pattern
Checking whether a string is a valid date, returning a boolean
Parsing text into a timestamp at midnight in the session time zone

query.title: Date and time conversion functions
query.syntax:
-- General forms
--   to_char(value, 'pattern')       -> text
--   to_date(text, 'pattern')        -> ?
--   to_timestamp(text, 'pattern')   -> ?
--   to_number(text, 'pattern')      -> numeric

-- Examples (different values)
SELECT to_char(now(), 'DD Mon YYYY');
SELECT to_date('15/08/2023', 'DD/MM/YYYY');
SELECT to_timestamp('2023-08-15 14:30', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI');

-- Common pattern tokens
--   YYYY year, MM month number, Mon abbreviated month name,
--   DD day of month, HH24 hour 0-23, MI minute, SS second

-- Gotchas
-- * The pattern describes how the input text is laid out; it is not validated
--   like a strict parser: extra or mismatched separators are often tolerated.
-- * Fields missing from the input take defaults (e.g. no day -> day 1).
-- * Out-of-range values raise an error (e.g. month 13), not NULL.
-- * No built-in boolean 'is valid date' function; wrap a cast in
--   exception handling (PL/pgSQL) or validate with a regex.
-- * For ISO-style text, a plain cast works: '2023-08-15'::date
-- * Check each function's return type in the docs before relying on it.
query.explanation: `to_date` and `to_timestamp` are the inverse of `to_char`: they parse a text value into a real date/timestamp according to an explicit format pattern, which matters whenever the incoming text is not already in Postgres’s default ISO 8601-ish format (day-first dates from a CSV export, for example).

questions.prompt: `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` is run on a date in May. What does it return?

choices.text: The month name as text, e.g. "May"
The numeric month, e.g. 5
A full date truncated to the first of the month
The number of months since order_date

query.title: Date/time functions
query.syntax:
-- General form
EXTRACT(field FROM source)   -- source: date, timestamp, time, interval
-- Returns numeric (PG 14+; double precision before 14)

-- Examples
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR  FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 2023
SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 11 (a number, not 'November')
SELECT EXTRACT(DOW   FROM DATE '2023-11-07');        -- 2 (Sunday = 0)
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM TIMESTAMP '2023-11-07 00:00'); -- seconds since 1970

-- Common fields: CENTURY, YEAR, QUARTER, MONTH, WEEK, DAY, DOW, ISODOW,
--   DOY, HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND, EPOCH
-- date_part('month', ts) is the older equivalent (returns double precision)

-- Gotchas:
-- * For a month NAME, use to_char(ship_date, 'Month') or 'Mon' -> text
--   ('Month' is blank-padded to 9 chars; use 'FMMonth' to trim)
-- * To round down to the 1st of the month, use date_trunc('month', ship_date)
-- * Months between dates: use age() and extract YEAR*12 + MONTH from it
-- * EXTRACT(MONTH FROM INTERVAL '14 months') -> 2 (the remainder, not 14)
-- * Grouping by month alone mixes years; group by YEAR and MONTH together
query.explanation: `EXTRACT` pulls a single numeric component (year, month, day, hour, day-of-week, and more) out of a date/time/interval value. It is commonly used for grouping reports by period, e.g. `GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)`.

questions.prompt: What does `date_trunc('month', order_date)` return?

choices.text: The month number as an integer, such as 5 for May
A timestamp rounded down to the first moment of that month
The date rounded to the nearest first-of-month
The month and year as text, such as '2024-05'

query.title: Date/time functions
query.syntax:
-- General form
date_trunc(field, source [, time_zone])
-- field: 'microseconds','milliseconds','second','minute','hour',
--        'day','week','month','quarter','year','decade','century','millennium'
-- Truncates (rounds DOWN) to the start of that unit; smaller fields are zeroed.

SELECT date_trunc('hour', timestamp '2023-11-17 14:47:09');
-- 2023-11-17 14:00:00

SELECT date_trunc('year', timestamp '2023-11-17 14:47:09');
-- 2023-01-01 00:00:00

-- Group rows per week
SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS wk, count(*)
FROM signups GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Never rounds to nearest: '2023-11-29' -> 2023-11-01, not 12-01.
-- * A date input is cast to timestamp(tz), so the result is a timestamp,
--   not a date; add ::date if you want a date.
-- * 'week' truncates to Monday (ISO weeks).
-- * To get a part as a number use extract(month FROM ts) / date_part.
-- * For text like '2023-11' use to_char(ts, 'YYYY-MM').
-- * With timestamptz, truncation uses the session TimeZone unless
--   the third time_zone argument is given (PG 12+).
-- * date_bin(stride, ts, origin) (PG 14+) buckets into arbitrary intervals.
query.explanation: Unlike `EXTRACT`, which pulls out a single numeric field, `date_trunc` zeroes out everything smaller than the given precision and returns a full timestamp back, which is what you want for grouping by calendar period while still being able to compare, sort, and display the result as a real date rather than a bare integer.

questions.prompt: After `UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING status;`, the returned value reflects the row before the update.

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING status; -- 'shipped'
query.explanation:
RETURNING on UPDATE reflects the new row

RETURNING on an UPDATE reports the row’s values after the update has been applied, not before, since it operates on the final row version the statement produces. If you need the old value too, you must capture it separately beforehand, for example with a `SELECT` in the same transaction, since RETURNING has no "OLD vs NEW" distinction the way a trigger does.

questions.prompt: Which psql meta-command lists views instead of ordinary tables?

choices.text: \dv
\dt
\dm
\di

query.title: psql meta-commands
query.syntax:
-- General form: backslash + d + object-type letter(s), optional modifiers and pattern
-- \d[S+] [pattern]   describe one relation, or list relations if no pattern
\dv                   -- list views in the search path
\dv+ sales.*          -- views in schema sales, with size/description
\dt inventory_*       -- ordinary tables matching a pattern
\di                   -- indexes
\dm                   -- materialized views
\ds                   -- sequences
\dE                   -- foreign tables
\d order_summary      -- describe a single view: columns plus its definition
\sv order_summary     -- show the view's CREATE statement

-- Letters combine: \dtv lists tables AND views together
-- S adds system objects:  \dvS  (includes pg_catalog/information_schema views)
-- + adds extra columns (size, description, persistence)
-- Patterns use * and ? wildcards; 'schema.name' qualifies by schema
-- Gotchas:
--   \dv does NOT include materialized views; use \dm for those
--   Without a pattern, only objects visible in search_path are listed
--   Meta-commands run in psql only, not as SQL from other clients
query.explanation: `\dv` lists views specifically, separate from `\dt` (ordinary tables), `\dm` (materialized views), and `\di` (indexes), following the same `\d<letter>` naming pattern used throughout psql’s describe commands.

questions.prompt: Which psql meta-command lists database roles (users and groups)?

choices.text: \du
\dn
\dt
\dv

query.title: psql meta-commands
query.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S][+] [pattern]

-- Examples:
\du                -- list roles with their attributes and memberships
\du app_*          -- only roles whose names start with app_
\du+               -- adds the Description column
\dg                -- same output as \du (kept for 'groups')

-- Related listing commands:
--   \dt  tables       \dv  views       \dn  schemas
--   \di  indexes      \ds  sequences   \df  functions
--   \l   databases    \dp  access privileges

-- Gotchas:
--  * Meta-commands start with a backslash and need no semicolon.
--  * They only work in psql, not in other clients or drivers.
--  * Patterns are wildcards (* and ?), not LIKE syntax.
--  * Add S to include system objects, e.g. \dtS.
--  * The SQL equivalent for roles is:
--      SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles;
--  * PostgreSQL has only roles; 'users' and 'groups' are roles
--    with or without LOGIN.
query.explanation: `\du` ("describe users") lists every role in the cluster along with its attributes, like whether it can log in, create databases, or is a superuser. Postgres does not distinguish "users" and "groups" as separate object types internally, both are roles, which is why this command shows both.

questions.prompt: What does `SHOW work_mem;` do?

choices.text: Resets work_mem to its default and prints the new value
Displays the current value of the work_mem configuration parameter
Shows how much memory the current query is using right now
Displays the work_mem value from postgresql.conf, ignoring SET

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.syntax:
SHOW work_mem;
SHOW ALL;
query.explanation: `SHOW parameter_name` is a read-only lookup of one server configuration setting as it applies to your current session, whether that value came from `postgresql.conf`, a per-role override, or a `SET` in the current session. `SHOW ALL` dumps every parameter at once; the underlying data is also queryable as a real table via `pg_settings`.

questions.prompt: What does `SET statement_timeout = '5s';` change?

choices.text: It changes the setting for every session on the server
It changes the setting for the rest of this session
It changes the setting for the next statement only
It changes the setting only until the current transaction ends

query.title: PostgreSQL runtime configuration settings
query.explanation: A plain `SET parameter = value` changes that setting for the rest of the current session only, leaving every other connection and the server default untouched; `RESET` reverts it. `SET LOCAL` narrows the scope further, to just the current transaction, which is useful for a one-off override you do not want to leak into later queries on the same connection.

questions.prompt: Given `arr = ARRAY[10, 20, 30, 40]`, what does `arr[2:3]` return?

query.title: Arrays
query.syntax:
-- General form: subscripts are 1-based; slices use lower:upper (inclusive)
-- array_expr[n]          -> single element
-- array_expr[lo:hi]      -> sub-array from lo to hi, both inclusive

SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d','e'])[4];      -- 'd'
SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d','e'])[2:4];    -- {b,c,d}
SELECT (ARRAY[5,6,7,8,9])[:2];               -- {5,6}   (omitted lower = start)
SELECT (ARRAY[5,6,7,8,9])[4:];               -- {8,9}   (omitted upper = end)

-- Gotchas:
-- * Indexing starts at 1, not 0.
-- * A slice always returns an array, even [3:3] -> {7}; plain [3] returns a scalar.
-- * Out-of-range subscript returns NULL; out-of-range slice returns an empty array '{}'.
-- * A literal ARRAY[...] needs parentheses before subscripting: (ARRAY[...])[i].
-- * If any dimension is written as a slice, all dimensions are treated as slices;
--   for 2-D arrays, arr[1:2][2] means arr[1:2][1:2].
-- * Arrays display with braces, e.g. {6,7}, not square brackets.
-- * array_lower/array_upper/array_length(arr, 1) report the bounds.
query.explanation: Postgres supports slice syntax on arrays, `arr[lower:upper]`, returning a sub-array containing the elements at those 1-based positions inclusive on both ends. Omitting either bound, `arr[:2]` or `arr[3:]`, slices from the start or through to the end respectively.

questions.prompt: What does a `LATERAL` subquery in a FROM clause let you do that a plain subquery cannot?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, top.*
FROM customers c,
LATERAL (
  SELECT * FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 1
) top;

choices.text: Run the subquery once and reuse its result for every row
Reference columns of earlier FROM items inside the subquery
Return rows even when the subquery finds nothing, like LEFT JOIN
Run the subquery in parallel with the outer query

query.title: Subqueries in the FROM clause
query.syntax:
-- General form: a LATERAL item may reference columns of FROM items listed before it
SELECT ...
FROM left_item alias,
     LATERAL (subquery using alias.col) sub_alias;

-- Explicit join form (same as comma for inner semantics)
SELECT ... FROM a CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...) s;

-- Example: latest 2 posts per author
SELECT au.username, p.title
FROM authors au
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT title FROM posts
  WHERE posts.author_id = au.author_id
  ORDER BY published_at DESC
  LIMIT 2
) p;

-- Keep outer rows with no match: LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true
SELECT d.dept_name, e.emp_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT emp_name FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.dept_id
  ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1
) e ON true;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Comma / CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops outer rows whose subquery returns nothing.
-- * The subquery is conceptually evaluated once per row of the preceding items.
-- * Only items to the LEFT can be referenced.
-- * Functions in FROM are implicitly lateral: FROM t, generate_series(1, t.n)
-- * Without LATERAL, referencing an earlier FROM item in a subquery is an error.
query.explanation: An ordinary subquery in FROM is planned once, in isolation, and cannot see columns from a sibling FROM item. Marking it `LATERAL` (implicit for functions, explicit for subqueries) lets it reference columns from FROM items listed before it, conceptually re-running the subquery once per row, which is exactly what you need for a "top N per group" query like fetching each customer’s most recent order.

questions.prompt: If you have a table literally named `order`, which of these is required to reference it?

choices.text: SELECT * FROM order;
SELECT * FROM "order";
SELECT * FROM 'order';
Nothing extra, order works fine unquoted

query.title: Identifiers and key words
query.syntax:
-- General form: wrap an identifier in double quotes
SELECT "column_name" FROM "table_name";

-- Reserved words must be quoted when used as identifiers
CREATE TABLE "user" (id int, "select" text);
SELECT "select" FROM "user" WHERE id = 1;

-- Schema-qualified: quote each part separately
SELECT * FROM public."group";

-- Gotchas:
-- 'text' in single quotes is a string literal, never an identifier
--   SELECT * FROM 'group';   -- syntax error
-- Unquoted names are folded to lower case:
--   MyTable = mytable, but "MyTable" is a different, case-sensitive name
-- Once created quoted with capitals, you must always quote it the same way
-- To include a double quote inside a name, write it twice: "a""b"
-- Non-reserved key words (e.g. name, value) may be used unquoted
-- quote_ident('group') returns the safely quoted form for dynamic SQL
-- Best practice: avoid reserved words as names to skip quoting entirely
query.explanation: `ORDER` is a reserved SQL keyword (it introduces `ORDER BY`), so using it unquoted as a table or column name causes a parse error. Wrapping it in double quotes tells Postgres to treat it strictly as an identifier rather than a keyword, letting you use otherwise-reserved words as names, though it is generally best avoided for readability.

questions.prompt: What does `pg_sleep(2)` do when called in a query?

choices.text: Pauses every session on the server for 2 seconds
Pauses the current session for 2 seconds, then returns
Pauses for 2 milliseconds before the query continues
Releases the session's locks, waits 2 seconds, then returns

query.title: Date/time functions and server utilities
query.syntax:
-- General form: delay the CURRENT session's execution
pg_sleep(seconds double precision)        -- returns void
pg_sleep_for(interval)                    -- PG 9.4+
pg_sleep_until(timestamp with time zone)  -- PG 9.4+

-- Examples
SELECT pg_sleep(0.5);                     -- half a second (fractions allowed)
SELECT pg_sleep_for('3 minutes');
SELECT pg_sleep_until('tomorrow 03:00');

-- Only the calling backend sleeps; other sessions keep running.
-- Argument is in SECONDS, not milliseconds: pg_sleep(1.5) = 1.5 s.
-- Effective resolution is platform-specific; 0.01 s is common.
-- Locks already held are NOT released while sleeping, so sleeping
-- inside a transaction can block other sessions.
-- statement_timeout still applies and can cancel a long sleep.
-- Called once per row if used in a SELECT list over a table:
--   SELECT pg_sleep(0.1) FROM generate_series(1,5);  -- ~0.5 s total
-- Handy for testing timeouts, lock waits, and monitoring scripts.
query.explanation: `pg_sleep(seconds)` simply pauses the calling backend for the given duration and then returns void; it does not affect any other session or the server as a whole. It is mostly a testing and demonstration tool, for example to deliberately hold a lock open in one session while observing blocking behavior from another.

questions.prompt: `SELECT random();` can return exactly 1.0.

query.title: Mathematical functions
query.syntax:
-- General form
random()                      -- double precision, 0.0 <= x < 1.0
random(min, max)              -- PG17+: integer/bigint/numeric, min <= x <= max (both inclusive)
random_normal(mean, stddev)   -- PG16+: normally distributed value
setseed(seed)                 -- seed between -1.0 and 1.0

-- Examples
SELECT floor(random() * 6)::int + 1 AS die_roll;   -- 1..6
SELECT random(10, 20);                             -- 10..20, PG17+
SELECT setseed(0.42); SELECT random();             -- repeatable sequence
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY random() LIMIT 3;  -- random sample (slow on big tables)

-- Gotchas
-- random() includes 0.0 but excludes 1.0 (half-open range)
-- floor(random() * n) gives 0..n-1; round() makes the end values half as likely
-- random() is VOLATILE: it is evaluated again for every row
-- setseed() affects only the current session
-- Not cryptographically secure; use pgcrypto gen_random_bytes() for secrets
-- For sampling large tables, consider TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM / BERNOULLI
query.explanation: `random()` returns a `double precision` value in the half-open range from 0 inclusive up to, but never including, 1. It takes no seed argument; to get a reproducible sequence for testing you call the separate `setseed(value)` function first, rather than passing a seed to `random()` itself.

questions.prompt: Why does inserting the literal 'don''t' (with two single quotes) store the text don't (with one apostrophe)?

choices.text: Two adjacent literals 'don' and 't' are joined into one
Inside a single-quoted literal, '' is the escape for one quote
The second quote is dropped as a typo, with a warning
It is invalid unless standard_conforming_strings is off

query.title: String constants and literals
query.syntax:
-- General form: a string constant is text enclosed in single quotes
'text here'

-- To include a single quote inside, write two adjacent single quotes
SELECT 'it''s here';            -- result: it's here
SELECT 'O''Brien''s pub';       -- result: O'Brien's pub
SELECT '''quoted''';            -- result: 'quoted'

-- Variations:
-- Escape string syntax (E prefix) also accepts backslash escapes
SELECT E'can\'t stop';          -- result: can't stop

-- Dollar quoting avoids doubling quotes entirely
SELECT $$won't need doubling$$;
SELECT $tag$a 'b' c$tag$;

-- Gotchas:
-- Double quotes (") delimit identifiers, not strings: "col" is a column name
-- Two literals separated only by whitespace that includes a newline are
--   concatenated: 'foo'
--   'bar' -> 'foobar' (but 'foo' 'bar' on one line is a syntax error)
-- With standard_conforming_strings = on (default), a backslash in '...'
--   is a literal backslash; use E'...' for backslash escapes
-- In application code, prefer bound parameters over manual quote escaping
query.explanation: The SQL standard (and Postgres by default) escapes an embedded single quote inside a plain string literal by doubling it, not with a backslash. Backslash escapes only work inside an `E'...'` "escape string" literal, and are not honored in a plain string unless the `standard_conforming_strings` setting has been turned off, which is not the modern default.

questions.prompt: users.email is stored in lower case and has a B-tree index. Which query finds a user by email faster?

choices.text: Compare email directly
choices.code: SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = 'user4242@example.com'

choices.text: Compare lower(email)
choices.code: SELECT id FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user4242@example.com'
choices.rationale: An index on email cannot answer a condition on lower(email), so the planner scans every row and calls lower() on each.

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 50,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 0.002 ms, B: 3.4 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.explanation:
Functions on indexed columns hide the index

A B-tree index on `email` stores `email` values, not `lower(email)` values, so a condition on the expression cannot use it. Compare the column itself, or create an expression index on `lower(email)` if case-insensitive lookups are needed.

questions.prompt: Which query checks faster whether customer 7 has any orders? (orders has 100,000 rows and no index on customer_id.)

choices.text: count(*) > 0
choices.code: SELECT count(*) > 0 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7
choices.rationale: count(*) has to read every matching row to finish the count, which means scanning the whole table.

choices.text: EXISTS
choices.code: SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7)

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 100,000-row table.
criterion.evidence: A: 2.3 ms, B: 0.002 ms median on PostgreSQL 17.11

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.explanation:
EXISTS stops at the first match

To answer "is there at least one?", `EXISTS` can stop as soon as it finds a row. `count(*)` must find every matching row before it can compare the count with zero.

questions.prompt: products.id is the primary key. Which query fetches product 4242 faster?

choices.text: Compare id as an integer
choices.code: SELECT sku FROM products WHERE id = 4242

choices.text: Cast id to text
choices.code: SELECT sku FROM products WHERE id::text = '4242'
choices.rationale: Casting the column to text means the primary key index on id no longer applies, so every row is cast and compared.

criterion.statement: Faster median execution time on a 50,000-row table.

query.title: Postgres · Easy
query.explanation:
Cast the value, not the column

An index can only serve a condition on the indexed column itself. `id::text = ...` applies a cast to every row. Compare `id` with an integer, casting the literal or parameter if needed, and the primary key index finds the row directly.

questions.prompt: products.sku has a B-tree index (C collation). Which query finds SKUs starting with SKU-0042 faster?

choices.text: left(sku, 8) = 'SKU-0042'
choices.code: SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE left(sku, 8) = 'SKU-0042'
choices.rationale: left(sku, 8) is an expression the index does not store, so every row is read and trimmed.

choices.text: sku LIKE 'SKU-0042%'
choices.code: SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE sku LIKE 'SKU-0042%'

query.title: Indexes and query planning
query.explanation: With the C collation (or a `text_pattern_ops` index), Postgres turns `LIKE 'prefix%'` into a range condition on the index. Wrapping the column in `left()` or `substr()` gives the same answer but forces a scan of every row.
query.syntax:
-- A B-tree index can serve an anchored prefix match when the
-- column is compared directly, not wrapped in a function.
-- General form:
--   WHERE col LIKE 'prefix%'
-- The planner rewrites it to a range: col >= 'prefix' AND col < 'prefiy'

CREATE INDEX orders_code_idx ON orders (code COLLATE "C");

-- Uses the index (Index/Bitmap scan):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE code LIKE 'ORD-77%';

-- Same idea, written as an explicit range:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE code >= 'ORD-77' AND code < 'ORD-78';

-- Cannot use a plain index on code (function hides the column):
--   WHERE substr(code, 1, 6) = 'ORD-77'
--   WHERE lower(code) LIKE 'ord-77%'
-- Fix: index the expression itself:
CREATE INDEX orders_code_lower_idx ON orders (lower(code));

-- Gotchas:
-- * Non-C collations: a default B-tree index cannot serve LIKE.
--   Use an operator class instead:
--   CREATE INDEX ON orders (code text_pattern_ops);
-- * Leading wildcard ('%77') cannot use B-tree; consider pg_trgm.
-- * ILIKE uses the index only when the prefix has no letters.
-- * Check with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) to confirm the plan.
